segments.text: Welcome back.
Day twenty-four.
For three weeks, most of what we've done has been about your head.
Thoughts, feelings, plans.
Today is about the rest of you.
Even a few minutes of movement, like a brisk walk or some stairs, can help a craving pass.
That's worth knowing, because it's a tool you carry everywhere, and it needs nothing but you.
It doesn't have to be exercise.
You don't have to enjoy it, or change your clothes, or be good at it.
A walk to the end of the street counts.
So do the stairs.
And about appetite, since a lot of people wonder.
It's common to feel hungrier, and some people put on a little weight after stopping.
That's normal.
Regular meals, water and some movement can help.
This isn't the moment for a strict diet.
Your body has done a great deal of adjusting these past weeks.
It deserves looking after, not policing.
If you're using nicotine replacement, follow the plan on the pack, and a pharmacist can help with any questions.
If cravings pick up after a step, that's okay.
Lean on your tools.
Let's try it now, if you're somewhere you can.
And if you'd rather stay sitting, that's fine.
You can do a smaller version right where you are.
First, notice how your body feels.
Any restlessness.
Any tightness.
Now move.
Stand up, if you can.
Roll your shoulders back.
Stretch your arms up, or out.
Shift your weight from one foot to the other.
Walk a few steps, if there's room.
Let your breathing pick up a little, in a way that feels comfortable for you.
And come to rest.
Notice your body again.
Has anything changed?
Even slightly?
That took under a minute.
So here's the idea for this week.
The next time a craving comes, move first.
Before you decide anything, before you argue with any passengers.
Five minutes, then see what's left of it.
In a moment, you'll pick two ways to move that fit your life as it really is.
Moving is one more tool in your kit.
I'll see you in a few days.
